controls.bloomToggleHint: Soft glow that spreads from bright areas (bloom).
controls.bloomThresholdHint: Only pixels brighter than this level contribute strongly to the glow.
controls.halationToggleHint: Colored glow around very bright edges (halation).
controls.finishToolsMistOutcome: Soften the whole image with a finished haze.
controls.finishToolsCrossOutcome: Turn point lights into a visible optical signature.
controls.finishToolsTextureOutcome: Add grain and falloff to make the image feel finished.
controls.finishToolsLensOutcome: Add subtle fringing and softness to break the digital clean edge.
controls.finishToolsMotionOutcome: Shape motion smear and trails while you judge in playback.
controls.artifactsSectionHint: Grain, vignette, glow, halation, and related film-look controls.
controls.sourceTrimSectionHint: Adjust the imported image before the film look—exposure, color, highlights, and shadows.
controls.compressionHint: Softens bright tones with a film-style shoulder curve. Not file or data compression.
controls.compressionRangeHint: Widens or narrows how much of the tonal range that softness affects (highlights through shadows).
controls.printContrastHint: Adds contrast in the print-style stage—separate from the main Contrast slider in the grading stack.
controls.rgbShiftToggleHint: Turn chromatic aberration on or off. It can break the image if pushed too far, so use it only when needed.
controls.grainRadialMixHint: Near 0: even grain. Near 1: stronger toward frame edges (not chromatic aberration). At 1 matches the previous default.
controls.lightShaftsToggleHint: Volumetric beams of light radiating from a point in the frame.
controls.shaftIntensityHint: Overall brightness of the light shafts. Zero means off.
controls.shaftDecayHint: How quickly the beams fade as they spread from the source.
controls.shaftOriginXHint: Horizontal position of the light source (0 = left, 1 = right).
controls.shaftOriginYHint: Vertical position of the light source (0 = top, 1 = bottom).
controls.crossFilterToggleHint: Star-shaped light streaks from bright points, like a physical cross-screen lens filter.
controls.crossFilterSpikesHint: Number of light spikes: 4-point (classic cross), 6-point (snow cross), or 8-point (sunny cross).
controls.crossFilterAngleHint: Rotates the spike pattern. 0° places the first spike pointing right.
controls.crossFilterLengthHint: How far the light spikes extend from bright sources.
controls.crossFilterThresholdHint: Only pixels brighter than this level produce spikes. Higher values limit the effect to the brightest points.
controls.crossFilterChromaticHint: Color dispersion along each spike, like light diffracting through a ruled grating.
controls.crossFilterSizeLimitHint: Suppresses streaks from large light sources. Higher values limit the effect to small point sources, excluding lamps, sun, or other area lights.
controls.crossFilterRandomnessHint: Controls what fraction of light sources produce streaks. Lower values create a sparse, selective effect.
controls.crossFilterHardModeOverrideHint: Hard Mode forces these values internally. Switch to Soft to control them manually.
controls.crossFilterMinSpacingHint: Reduces the intensity of nearby overlapping streaks while preserving the light cluster shape. Use this to declutter dense groups such as chandeliers.
controls.dustAmountHint: Adds random dust particles over the image, like aged film stock.
controls.scratchAmountHint: Adds vertical film scratches that drift across the frame.
controls.shutterAngleHint: 180° is the normal-source baseline with no added blur; above 180° adds a slow-shutter extension.
controls.trailIntensityHint: Extends afterimages beyond the shutter window; it only affects active slow-shutter motion.

Turn on step-by-step WebGL only if you want a closer match to the preview. .cube LUT is preferred; Params are approximated in ffmpeg — lutIntensity, bloom, halation, and split-tone details may not match. ffmpeg and ffprobe must be on PATH.
batch.tipJobVideoWebGlOnly: Only WebGL frame-by-frame export (slower) for a closer preview match. Fast one-pass ffmpeg is being prepared and hidden from the UI. ffmpeg and ffprobe must be on PATH.
batch.tipSourcesImagesFolder: Only .jpg / .jpeg / .png in that folder (not subfolders by default in UI copy). Not for video conversion.
batch.tipSourcesVideoFile: Import limit: up to 4K and max {maxSec}s. ffmpeg and ffprobe must be on PATH.

batch.tipApplyEditGradeToBatch: Copies slider and tone values from Edit into this export (same as “Send grade to Export”). After changing preset, preset values apply until you sync. LUT (.cube) is not copied here — use “Advanced: Grade JSON” below.
batch.tipFilenameSuffix: Inserted before the extension. Example: -graded → IMG0001-graded.jpg. Empty = no suffix. Use a different folder than sources to avoid overwriting.
batch.tipVideoOutputNaming: Output file name is original stem + -graded.mp4. Max output FHD · {fps} fps.
batch.tipWebglAccurate: When on, seeks each frame and grades via readPixels — very slow but closest to Edit. Off (default) uses fast ffmpeg one-pass (approximate). .cube LUT preferred; Params approximated in ffmpeg.
batch.tipKeyboardShortcuts: ⌘1 / ⌘2 (Ctrl on Windows) switch tabs. On Export, ⌘↵ runs “{imagesLabel}” or “Export video”. ⇧⌘↵ retries failed items only (photos). ⇧⌘Y resumes. Esc cancels.

entries.v103Title: Filmtone Desktop v1.0.3 — export quality and HDR source handling
entries.v103HdrHandling: HDR PQ, HLG, and wide-gamut source detection is clearer during import and export, with user-facing messages that explain practical brightness or color risk without developer jargon.
entries.v103BundledVideoTools: Desktop now bundles the video toolchain needed for normal exports, reducing dependency on separate developer or Homebrew setup for HDR-to-SDR preparation paths.
entries.v103PreviewExportTrust: Video export starts closer to the visible preview grade, keeps trusted source frame rate and geometry, and writes full-range BT.709 output so mist, bloom, halation, and highlight rolloff shift less at encode time.
entries.v103DefaultLook: New sessions and old grade imports without preset identity now start from Neutral / Clean Base with the shared soft-finish baseline.
entries.v102Title: Filmtone Desktop v1.0.2 — safer video export recovery
entries.v102FfmpegPipeRecovery: Broken ffmpeg pipe failures are caught and surfaced through the normal export failure path instead of leaving the renderer waiting on stale writes.
entries.v102ExportSessionIsolation: Each video export now has its own session id, so stale start, frame, finish, or abort messages from older exports cannot affect the active job.
entries.v102PreviewExportTrust: The current WebGPU preview/export contract stays aligned while export hardening continues, including low-end grain and offscreen render refinements.
entries.v101Title: Filmtone Desktop v1.0.1 — preview trust and cleaner write-out
entries.v101HighlightPreview: Bright footage is steadier in preview, with highlights that hold their shape more naturally while you judge the finished mood.
entries.v101CrossFilterPreview: Cross Filter is easier to tune live, with more reliable brightness onset, chromatic split, and spacing behavior on moving footage.
entries.v101ExportSidecar: Desktop exports can write a .filmtone-session.json sidecar so the finishing setup can be inspected, saved, and reopened later.
entries.v101WriteOutSurface: The write-out tab uses a cleaner glass surface with clearer controls, fields, preset tiles, and dividers.
entries.v100Title: Filmtone Desktop v1.0 — the first public release
entries.v100WebgpuPreview: Preview has been reworked end-to-end. Bright highlights now hold their shape more naturally, so it is easier to judge the finished look right on screen.
entries.v100CrossFilterPreviewControls: Cross Filter now responds live while you preview your image. Fine-tune the brightness that triggers the streaks, how much they split into color, and how close they sit, and the result updates immediately.
entries.v100SignedNotarizedDmg: The macOS build is now signed and notarized by Apple. The download page and the in-app update prompt both point to this v1.0.0 release, so installing is simple and trusted.
entries.v100DesktopFirstReleaseScope: v1.0 focuses on improving Desktop preview. The browser demo, video export, and photo batch export continue to work exactly as they did before.
entries.v062HardOnlySurface: Cross Filter now ships as a single, well-tuned mode, trimmed down so it is easier to reach for without hesitation.
entries.v062StateNormalization: Old settings files and shared links open correctly and automatically fit into the current mode — nothing looks different from what you originally saved.
entries.v062DiscreteSpikes: Pick the number of streaks in one tap: 4, 6, or 8.
entries.v061Title: Update notifications are back, and night-scene glow feels better
entries.v061LaunchUpdateBanner: Filmtone again shows a banner at launch when a newer version is available.
entries.v061PreviewRecoveryAfterExport: Fixed cases where preview could stay black after exporting — preview now recovers on its own whenever it is needed.
entries.v061GlowBlackMistRetune: Glow in Black-Mist-style night scenes now keeps its shape instead of flattening into blown-out white patches.
entries.v061HardCrossFilterSpacing: Cross Filter streaks now separate cleanly even when bright highlights sit close together.
entries.v060Title: Cross Filter arrives, and video feels smoother
entries.v060CrossFilter: Cross Filter adds lens-style star streaks to bright points in your image. Dial in the strength, the number of streaks, the angle, the length, the brightness that triggers them, and a touch of color split, to find your own look.
entries.v060VideoCompareUx: Video compare and review feel smoother — compare mode is easier to exit, slider resets are easier to find, and a faster playback option makes quick checks more natural.
entries.v060ThumbnailLoadingPolish: Leading thumbnails now pick a brighter frame automatically, so clips that fade in look right from the very first glance. Loading text has also been aligned with the rest of the app.
entries.v060PersistentProxyCache: Desktop can now keep preview data for heavy footage on your computer, so opening the same clip again is faster. You can let Filmtone manage the space automatically or clear it yourself whenever you want.
entries.v051ProgressiveLoading: ProRes, 4K HEVC, and other demanding formats preview the moment you drop them in. Filmtone prepares an optimized copy in the background and reuses it at export, so you never wait on the same clip twice.
entries.v051RingBufferMotionBlur: Motion blur has been rebuilt with real shutter-angle control (0° to 720°), and a separate Trail Intensity slider for stylised streaks, so you can shape the look more intuitively.
entries.v051PortraitVideo: 9:16 vertical clips now display full-frame. The side areas are filled with a softly blurred version of the footage itself, so portrait video looks polished without any manual setup.
entries.v051ComparisonModeFix: Fixed Before / After compare so only the graded side shows motion blur — the original stays clean, and no ghost frames carry over when you switch modes.
entries.v050Title: Grain that looks like the real thing
entries.v050GrainV3: The grain engine has been rebuilt from the ground up — each film stock now has its own natural clumping, texture size, and color-noise character, so Kodak and Fuji grain no longer look the same.
entries.v050Diffusion: A new Diffusion slider wraps your image in a soft, milky haze — like shooting through a Pro-Mist filter — gently lifting contrast and flattering skin tones.
entries.v050CineStillHalation: CineStill 800T now loads clean by default. Dial in the iconic red halation glow yourself with the slider whenever you want it.
entries.v050PresetRecalibration: All 10 film stock presets have been hand-tuned with matching grain size and diffusion, so each look feels true to the actual film it was inspired by.
entries.v050UiReorganization: The Pro panel has been reorganized so the controls you use most are immediately visible. Effects still being refined are tucked away until they are ready.
entries.v045BloomHalationRework: Bloom and halation have been completely reimagined — glow spreads more naturally, highlights behave at any slider position, and the overall look is closer to real film. Existing grades may shift slightly.
entries.v045PresetRecalibration: All 10 film stock presets have been recalibrated so bloom and halation feel natural and true to each stock's character.
entries.v044ProresLoadAndExport: You can now import, grade, and export ProRes MOV files — including LOG footage straight from your camera. Filmtone prepares the file automatically on the way in.
entries.v044Dci4kInput: Cinema-resolution files (DCI 4K and above) are now fully supported as video input.
entries.v043FasterHevcExport: 4K footage that used to take three minutes to export now finishes in under 45 seconds — up to 4× faster for demanding camera files.
entries.v043AutoSourceOptimize: Filmtone quietly optimizes heavy camera files before grading so export runs at full speed. Lighter files skip this step entirely.
entries.v043OptimizationProgress: A progress bar now shows while Filmtone prepares a heavy source file, so you know exactly what is happening before export begins.
entries.v042ProPanelVocabulary: Pro panel labels have been updated to plain photography language — Film texture, Color fringing, Source adjustments — so controls are easier to understand at a glance.
entries.v042BloomThresholdHint: Bloom's threshold slider now shows a brief tip explaining which highlight tones trigger the glow.
entries.v042VideoTransport: Video preview now has full playback controls — play, pause, scrub, timecode display, and Space bar toggle.
entries.v041ProToneLabels: The tone section now uses everyday language — highlight softness, tone span, print snap — with short hover descriptions so every slider is self-explanatory.
entries.v041SliderTooltipReset: All sliders now show a tip reminding you that tapping the label resets that control to default.
entries.v040Title: Film process controls and a cleaner workflow
entries.v040FilmProcess: New film process controls let you shape compression, tonal range, print contrast, and color cast — what you see in the preview is exactly what exports.
entries.v040QuickProIa: Quick mode takes you straight to the look; Pro mode surfaces the full set of film process, texture, and source controls — each mode shows only what you need.
entries.v040FilmStockPicker: Film stocks are now grouped by category, so finding Velvia 50 among cinematic and other options takes seconds instead of scrolling.
entries.v040PanelStability: Desktop no longer loses your process settings when you switch between photo and video tabs.
entries.v040ShareCompat: Shared links and exported grades remain fully compatible with older versions while carrying the new process fields when available.
entries.v031Title: Export in the browser — and better reliability across the board
entries.v031WebVideoExportBeta: You can now export a graded video clip directly from the browser — no download required to test your look on short footage.
entries.v031WebBrowserReliability: Browser export is more reliable, and a clearer message now guides Safari users toward Chrome, Edge, or the Desktop app when needed.
entries.v031FinderThumb: Exported MP4s no longer show a black thumbnail in Finder or Quick Look — previews now display the actual graded frame.
entries.v031MovHandling: Video import now handles a wider range of camera files, including MOV files that some cameras save without standard type information.
entries.v030Title: Cleaner export and faster preset discovery
entries.v030ExportIa: Photo batch export and single video export are now clearly separated — tabs, panel, and toolbar all point you to the right place.
entries.v030ExportSource: The image or clip you are actively grading carries over into export as the default, so wrong-file exports are much less likely.
entries.v030VisualPolish: The export panel and the editing view share the same visual language, making the transition between grading and exporting feel seamless.
entries.v030PresetSearch: Type to search film stock presets — no more scrolling through the full list to find a specific look.
entries.v030ExportBusyPause: Video preview pauses automatically while a file is exporting so nothing looks out of sync.
entries.v030WebPreview: The browser demo preview is taller and better framed, giving a closer impression of the Desktop experience.
entries.v020Title: Two LUTs at once, redesigned export, and faster video
entries.v020DualLut: Load two LUT files simultaneously — use the first to convert your LOG footage to a standard look, the second for your creative grade, each with its own intensity control.
entries.v020LutSync: LUTs you set in the editing tab now follow through to export. A status indicator shows at a glance whether your grade is in sync, out of sync, or partially applied.
entries.v020InlineExportPanel: Export now lives right alongside your grade in a compact panel — the image stays visible the whole time, no more multi-step wizard.
entries.v020WebCodecsReEnabled: Video export in the browser has been restored with improved color accuracy and hardware-accelerated performance.
entries.v020UpdateNotify: A banner appears inside the app when a new version of Filmtone is available.
entries.v020PackageRefactor: Under-the-hood restructuring to keep the app fast and stable as new features are added.
entries.v013FrameLogSuppression: Video export now runs more cleanly in the background, with a small performance improvement on longer clips.
entries.v012VideoColorShift: Fixed a color shift that could appear in exported video, ensuring graded footage matches what you see on screen.
entries.v011FfmpegPath: Fixed an issue where the Desktop app (DMG) could fail to process video after installation.
entries.v010BatchExport: Apply any preset to an entire folder of photos and export them all at once as JPEG or PNG.
entries.v010VideoExport: Export a video clip with your chosen grade baked in.
entries.v010FourPresets: Four film stock looks to start: Kodak Portra 400, Fuji Pro 400H, Kodak Ektar 100, and Ilford HP5 Plus.
entries.v010BrowserDemo: Try any preset on your own photos in the browser before downloading the Desktop app.
entries.iosV11Title: Filmtone for iPhone v1.1 — source transparency
entries.iosV11HdrNotice: HDR and wide-gamut clips now show an in-app notice so you can see how iOS will handle the source before export.
entries.iosV11OpticsMetadata: Camera and optics metadata can feed the vignette model for more physically accurate corner falloff on supported clips.
entries.iosV11SidecarJson: Exports include a sidecar JSON alongside the media with grade, preset, and camera context for cleaner round trips with Desktop.
entries.iosV11ProresAppleLog: ProRes and Apple Log import handling is clearer, and unsupported conversion paths are recorded in the sidecar instead of being hidden.
entries.iosV10Title: Filmtone for iPhone v1.0 — first App Store release
entries.iosV10Presets: Film-stock presets are available on iPhone as the starting point for quick local grading.
entries.iosV10QuickControls: Quick controls cover exposure, contrast, and saturation for fast adjustment on the device.
entries.iosV10DualLut: Camera Profile and Film Look LUT slots support more precise source and creative workflows.
entries.iosV10ExportShare: Export, save to Photos, and share are available from the iPhone workflow.

portfolio-renewal-2026.title: Giving up dark/light dual-mode — how a WebGPU shader's hardcoded value chose the entire site's palette
portfolio-renewal-2026.summary: Unifying the portfolio's background to a single sheet was, in fact, decided by the technology from the start. A WebGPU-driven motion-dot shader bakes its clear color as `[0.82, 0.82, 0.82, 1.0]`, so any divergence from that value flickers the background on every scroll. The dual-mode path was already closed. This is a record of accepting that constraint as a method — and what we cut to make it work (CSS scrims, theme toggles, full-surface Liquid Glass).
portfolio-renewal-2026.metaDescription: An editorial record of dropping dark/light dual-mode in favor of a single light substrate. Starting from a WebGPU shader's hardcoded constraint, readability moved into the shader pipeline itself, with cut features and preserved exceptions made explicit.

mobile-safari-touch-controller.title: Solving iOS Safari's 100vh problem with a single CSS variable — why we lower visualViewport into :root
mobile-safari-touch-controller.summary: iOS Safari's URL bar collapse breaks `100vh`, opening gaps in the background during scroll. Distributing the value through React context or props collapsed early in an environment where SSR, client, and shaders coexist. Instead, a small client component subscribed to `window.visualViewport` writes to `:root` CSS variables (`--vvh` / `--vvw` / `--vv-offset-*`), and CSS, JSX, and shaders all read from the same source. A record of a quiet, single-source-of-truth pattern that simply does not break.
mobile-safari-touch-controller.metaDescription: How to solve iOS Safari's 100vh breakage with the `visualViewport` API published to `:root` CSS variables — a robust pattern derived from the failure of distributing the same value through React context across SSR, client, and shaders.

journal-typography-wordmark-system.title: Why our wordmark lives as SVG paths, not a font — a pipeline that re-carves only the glyphs we need from Geist Sans
journal-typography-wordmark-system.summary: Identity needed a carved wordmark, not a font. Off-the-shelf display faces couldn't reach the flat-top A, the K junction gap, or the C terminal cuts at the Bezier-control-point level. We built an extract → modify → build pipeline: it takes Geist Sans Medium 500, isolates A, K, C, T, H, B, M, modifies their letterforms, and freezes them as SVG paths. The coexistence with Jost is still unresolved — leaving that visible is part of the record.
journal-typography-wordmark-system.metaDescription: Why a portfolio wordmark lives as SVG paths rather than a font, plus the pipeline that carves only the needed glyphs out of Geist Sans. A typographic editorial choice — giving up reversibility to gain identity.

filmtone-motion-180-shutter-baseline.title: Making 180° the no-op baseline — rewriting Filmtone's motion blur to the industry standard
filmtone-motion-180-shutter-baseline.summary: Footage shot on iPhones or cinema cameras already carries roughly 180° of shutter blur. Adding another 180° pass on top double-blurs the image. So we rebuilt the math: 180° is now the no-op baseline, and only angles above 180° act as a shutter-window extension. We checked RED, Foundry Nuke, Blender, Houdini, and After Effects, and aligned with the industry-standard exposure-as-fraction definition. A record of that judgment and its implementation.
filmtone-motion-180-shutter-baseline.metaDescription: How Filmtone's motion-blur math was rewritten so that 180° is the no-op baseline. Researching RED, Nuke, Blender, Houdini, and AE, we aligned shutter angle with the industry standard of exposure duration — and threaded the same math through WebGL, WebGPU, and Swift.

filmtone-dual-lut-pipeline.title: Splitting Source LUT from Look LUT — Filmtone's two-lane color processing architecture
filmtone-dual-lut-pipeline.summary: "One LUT for everything" broke quickly. A camera transform (Apple Log → Rec.709) and a creative look (a film treatment) play different roles. When you swap source footage, the Source LUT should clear, but the Look should stay. So Filmtone splits them: `inputLut` (Source) and `creativeLut` (Look) live in separate slots. The export order goes input → grade → tone compression → glow → grain → creative. Each LUT has its own intensity slider. A record of that two-lane color pipeline.
filmtone-dual-lut-pipeline.metaDescription: Why Filmtone separates inputLut (Source Profile/Camera) from creativeLut (Look) in two slots. Covers the source-replacement logic, the export order, and the independent intensity sliders that came with the architecture.

filmtone-cross-platform-color-parity.title: Sharing one math layer across WebGL/WebGPU preview and Swift export to keep colors identical
filmtone-cross-platform-color-parity.summary: Filmtone's preview runs in browsers (WebGL/WebGPU); the export runs in iOS Swift. The naive approach — implement the same math three times — breaks somewhere every time. Instead, we keep color transforms, motion blur, and exposure math in TypeScript inside `packages/film-lab-renderer`, and the Swift side mechanically picks them up via `bun run generate:filmtone-ios-swift`. A record of holding cross-platform color parity through structure, not discipline.
filmtone-cross-platform-color-parity.metaDescription: How Filmtone keeps colors identical across WebGL, WebGPU, and Swift export — color transforms, motion blur, and exposure math live in TypeScript, with Swift code generated from it. A cross-platform single-source-of-truth pattern.

filmtone-capacitor-native-bridge.title: Capacitor as a creative-tool host — nine native plugin methods that make Filmtone iOS work
filmtone-capacitor-native-bridge.summary: Filmtone iOS is a Capacitor hybrid app, but a creative tool needs more than HTML5 affords. Through `FilmtoneMediaPlugin`, nine native methods cover photo-library picking, LUT loading, native rendering, Live Activity, cancellation, and memory pressure response. The app reaches into PhotoLibrary, Core Image, and ActivityKit directly. A record of where we drew the web/native boundary.
filmtone-capacitor-native-bridge.metaDescription: How Filmtone iOS uses Capacitor as a host for a creative tool — nine native plugin methods (pickSource / pickLutFile / probeSource / runExport / Live Activity / cancelExport / and more) that bridge web and iOS without drowning in HTML5 limits.

filmtone-app-store-v12-shipping.title: Shipping Filmtone v1.2 to the App Store as a solo dev — fastlane, gym, and ASC traps that I had to fix
filmtone-app-store-v12-shipping.summary: Filmtone v1.2's App Store submission didn't go through on the first pass. fastlane 2.233's gym was passing authentication args into both `xcargs` and `export_xcargs`, breaking IPA export with `Exit status: 64`. Then deliver didn't include `release_notes`, so ASC rejected the review submission for missing `whatsNew`. I fixed the Fastfile each time and ended up factoring a `submit_review` lane that resubmits the existing build alone. A record of where the release pipeline broke and how a solo dev patched it.
filmtone-app-store-v12-shipping.metaDescription: How shipping Filmtone v1.2 to the App Store hit two fastlane bugs (gym double-passing auth args, deliver missing whatsNew) and how a solo dev patched the Fastfile to recover. A real-world record of indie iOS release engineering.

motionStudies.indexTitle: Motion Studies — single-purpose motion vocabulary, written one at a time
motionStudies.indexSummary: Independent of whether each one ships into the portfolio body, here is where motion vocabulary is isolated and written down — one technique per study, with the judgements, what was cut, and the technical constraints documented before the implementation.
motionStudies.metaDescription: Motion Studies index — Renewal 2026 motion vocabulary broken down into single-purpose R&D pieces.

signal-stroke-relay.title: The relay sensation cannot be built from separate animations — a Theatre.js timeline referenced by multiple layers with phase offsets
signal-stroke-relay.summary: The feeling of "a single motion traveling across layers" disappears the moment you write separate animations per layer. It only emerges when multiple layers reference the same motion with different offsets and eases. We held a single Theatre.js timeline as the "stem" of the gesture, with each layer reading it as its own "dialect" — a record of that structure.
signal-stroke-relay.metaDescription: A motion study on building the relay sensation — multiple layers referencing one Theatre.js timeline with phase-offset eases — and why separate animations cannot reach it.

staged-emphasis-payoff.title: How to keep a payoff in a three-line headline reveal — give the last stage a different ease
staged-emphasis-payoff.summary: Three lines on the same ease arrive together and the meaning scatters. Three lines on three different eases overwhelm and the weight becomes unreadable. Bind them as a family, assign them to early / mid / late stages, and reserve a different ease for the final stage — the payoff. We cap the number of stages at three. A pacing study with that constraint as the design.
staged-emphasis-payoff.metaDescription: A motion study on pacing three-line headline reveals — using the family / stage / payoff vocabulary, with a separate ease reserved for the final stage.

boiling-poster-aperture.title: A poster reveal that feels like wet paper — a boil noise that displaces only the rim (touch the interior and the paper-feel collapses)
boiling-poster-aperture.summary: A CSS `clip-path` reveals a poster with mechanical, hard edges. For a paper-like bleed, we hold a time-evolving boil field as low-frequency noise in WebGL and use it to displace only the mask's rim. The interior moves zero pixels. The counterintuitive rule: displace the interior even slightly, and paper turns to jelly.
boiling-poster-aperture.metaDescription: A motion study on revealing a poster with paper-like bleed using a boil noise field and displacement — confined to the rim only, with the interior held completely still as a counterintuitive rule.

temporal-echo-residue.title: Keeping a stopped motion's echo alive at 5–10% opacity — designing residue without collapsing into VFX
temporal-echo-residue.summary: We write the subjective feeling of "the screen has stopped, but something is still moving" as a mechanism. The last N frames are held in a buffer and decay exponentially, contributing 5–10% to the shader output. Push it to 20% and the editorial frame collapses into VFX, drawing attention away from the lead motion. Hold the echo internally; restrain how much of it is visible.
temporal-echo-residue.metaDescription: A motion study on designing residue — keeping the echo of a stopped motion alive in the shader output at 5–10% mix, with a hard cap to prevent collapse into VFX.

sections.text: Why we collapsed to a single light substrate

The first decision in Renewal 2026 was to make the background one. Not a dark/light pair, not a per-section theme. A single light substrate sits underneath, and reading, work, and motion all have to live on top of it.

The reason starts on the technical side. The motion-dot background runs WebGPU and writes its own clear color every frame to hold 60fps. That clear color is float-typed and hard-coded to `[0.82, 0.82, 0.82, 1.0]`. If the site disagreed with that color, the screen would flicker between two stages on every scroll.

// packages/motion-dot/src/main.ts
bgColor: [0.82, 0.82, 0.82, 1.0]

Which means a dark site is not on the table — not without rewriting the shader pipeline. Whether you call that a constraint or a stance is a matter of attitude. I chose the second. Holding every category on a single light surface was a stronger editorial position than producing a dark mode would have been.
Readability lives in a shader, not in a CSS scrim

Light text on a moving dot field gets noisy. The first attempt was the obvious one — drop a translucent panel under each block via `::before`. Readable, but lethal as an editorial surface. Every section gained a visible rectangle.

The fix lived in the shader. Sections opt-in via `data-readability`. `useReadabilityRegions` watches them through IntersectionObserver, weights by visible area, and lerps the dominant scalar into a CSS variable `--motion-dot-readability`. The motion-dot fragment pipeline reads that scalar and dims itself. CSS covers nothing.

<header data-readability="focus">…</header>
<section data-readability="reading">…</section>
After that, the rectangles were gone. The text and the background sit on the same plane — the background just gets quieter where reading is happening.
Liquid Glass stays, but only on the chrome

We banned `backdrop-filter` from body content as a rule. The navigation chrome, on the other hand, kept its Liquid Glass — it reads visualViewport and refracts. Glass belongs to the moving subject, not to the page. It never lands on top of reading.
Body uses the data-readability shader pipeline. Chrome uses Liquid Glass. Splitting them physically meant their responsibilities stopped colliding.
What was cut

items: The dark/light dual mode toggle (lost its meaning the moment substrate became one)
Section-level glass scrims (readability moved to the shader scalar)
Decorative panels and gradient overlays in body content
Per-section route-accent variations (only the chrome accent remains)

sections.text: Exceptions kept on purpose

Filmtone and Photography stay on their own systems. Filmtone is, as a product, a dark-UI app — it scopes itself with `.dark`. Photography would be eaten by its own imagery on a light substrate, so we flip the surface locally with `body:has(.photography-page)`. These are explicit exceptions, not omissions.
What is still open
motion-dot is WebGPU-first; the WebGL2 fallback gives up density. Whether a thinner background on lower-end devices reads as 'natural' or as 'weak' isn't fully decided yet.

The other open question is what happens the day a 'night chapter' has to enter the site. Today there is no such plan, but partitioning the substrate later would be a major rebuild. I'm leaving this here as acknowledged debt.
The problem

iOS Safari grows and shrinks its URL bar with scroll. `100vh` resolves to the expanded height and freezes there. By itself that's tolerable; in practice the body height, the motion-dot canvas full-bleed, and the Liquid Glass chrome's fixed position all start moving on different bases.

The visible failure is that, the moment the URL bar collapses, the motion-dot leaves a 64-px strip of empty space at the bottom. A background that doesn't reach the bottom of the page is editorially fatal.
The fix — publish once, consume from CSS variables
The implementation is intentionally small. A single client component, `VisualViewportVars`, subscribes to `window.visualViewport` and writes the values straight onto `:root` as CSS variables.

The motion-dot canvas reads `height: var(--vvh)` directly. The Liquid Glass chrome's fixed top becomes `top: calc(var(--vv-offset-top, 0px) + 1rem)`. Neither knows about the other; both fall from the same source of truth.
Where safe-area meets it

Notch and home-indicator insets come from `env(safe-area-inset-*)` — a separate axis from visualViewport. Only header and footer padding consume it; the motion-dot canvas explicitly extends past safe-area to fill the screen. The two systems are kept apart on purpose.
What this note does not cover

This piece covers visual-viewport delivery and the safe-area boundary only. A 44-pixel touch target audit and the touch-version of the keyboard-only HUDs are separate R&D and are not yet in source. They will be written up in the next wave.

items: Comprehensive 44-pixel touch target audit (audit tool not yet built)
Touch versions of keyboard-only HUDs in Filmtone and the experiments
Cross-checking visualViewport behavior on Android Chrome

sections.text: What we learned

Putting one global source of truth on `:root` as CSS variables is unsexy and durable. Shaders read it, JSX reads it, layouts read it. As more layers were added, nothing fell out of sync. Distributing the same values via React context or props broke far more often.
Why a wordmark at all

The C-arc + 工 logomark was designed as a modern personal kamon and works at small to medium sizes. It loses force when an editorial hero needs to fill a hero band and announce whose site this is. That role belongs to a different typographic device.
Two paths: (1) drop in an off-the-shelf display face, or (2) take a base typeface and carve it into a wordmark of our own. The first is fast but anonymous. We chose the second.
The pipeline — extract, modify, build

items: extract-glyphs.ts — extracts only the glyphs needed for CHIBA / TAKUMI from Geist Sans Medium 500 (.otf) as SVG paths
modify-glyphs.ts — applies hand-picked carvings: A flat-top, K junction gap, C terminal cuts, T extension, H optical center, B ink trap, M thinning
build-wordmark.ts — composes the modified paths into CHIBA / TAKUMI and writes them into `branding.wordmark.{primaryPaths,secondaryPaths}` in `portfolio.ts`

sections.text: At runtime, `BrandWordmark` renders the path arrays as fill-based SVG. Color is `currentColor`; weight and color stay in CSS.
Why path-baked, not font-subset

A subsetted web font is still a font — moving a single vertex isn't an option. SVG paths give you a flat A top, a junction gap on K, terminal cuts on C, all as ordinary math on Bezier control points. Reversibility is lost; uniqueness is the trade.
Honesty about the in-progress part

As of Renewal 2026, Jost is not fully removed. `apps/web/src/app/fonts.ts` still exports Jost 800, referenced inside `--font-family-display`. `font-mono` usages also remain. The full migration to a single display family is queued for the next wave.

The wordmark is therefore a first step. The logotype layer was rebuilt in isolation, ahead of the broader typography clean-up that has yet to land. Writing it down while it is still in motion is the point of this study.
What it taught us

items: The base face shapes how much carving room you get. Geist's neutrality made it pleasant to modify
Carvings should be intentional and few — A and K were touched, O and U were left alone, fixed at the start
Persist outputs in a form the site can actually draw. Not .otf, not .woff2 — SVG path data inside the data layer

sections.text: What we tried to make

The feeling of a single stroke that gets relayed across spaces — not as duplicated animations, but as multiple layers referencing one Theatre.js timeline. The same gesture, picked up by other layers with different eases, produces the relay.
The technical key

items: One Theatre.js keyframe playback as the master
Each relay layer reads the same timeline time with its own offset and ease
The phase difference between layers is what reads as 'the relay'

sections.text: What we cut

Early versions wrote a separate animation for each layer. The relay never appeared — the layers just looked unrelated. Same vocabulary across layers is the whole point, and a shared timeline is what guarantees it.
Where it could land
Hero stroke transitions, line elements during section changes. Whether it actually ships in the body is a separate decision; here it lives as documented vocabulary.
What we tried to make

Three headline lines on the same ease arrive together. Three lines on three different eases lose meaning. The aim is for the final line to carry a payoff — a small but distinct landing — without making the others noisy.
Vocabulary

items: family — share a common ease across the group
stage — assign positions (early / mid / late) within the family
payoff — give the final stage a different ease (light overshoot, soft residue)

sections.text: What we cut
Giving each line a slightly different ease was abandoned — too much information, no readable weight. The harder constraint was 'never use more than three stages.' That kept the payoff legible.
Where it could land
Hero title stagger, Filmtone step reveals, photography caption sequencing. Anywhere the same ease stretches across multiple beats.
What we tried to make

A poster reveal that opens the way paper bleeds through paper. CSS clip-path delivers only hard edges; a paper-like 'boil' isn't reachable. WebGL holds a boil field — a low-frequency noise field running on its own time — and the aperture's edge is displaced by it.
Structure

items: boil field — low-frequency noise plus a time phase, the 'simmering' surface
alpha-mask-gate — the reveal progress (0..1) for the poster
edge displacement — only the gate's rim is perturbed by the boil field

sections.text: What we cut

Pushing the boil amplitude high made the surface look like jelly, not paper. We confined the displacement to the rim and forbade modulating the interior. The moment the inside wobbles, the paper character is gone.
Where it could land
First-time poster-style reveals, Filmtone sample swaps, journal cover transitions.
What we tried to make

Carry the residue of motion past the moment it ends. The previous frames don't disappear instantly; they decay, and if new motion enters before the decay is over, the residue interferes with it. The screen is still — but something hasn't finished moving.
Structure

items: echo family — a buffer of N frames captured after the primary motion ends
decay — each captured frame loses energy exponentially over time
residue — if new motion arrives before decay completes, the remaining residue is added back into it

sections.text: What we cut

Visualizing echoes as ghost trails was abandoned. Visible ghosts read as VFX and pull the page out of the editorial register. The echo is kept numerically but contributes only a thin 5–10% of opacity to the shader output.
Where it could land
Section transitions, the trailing edge of scrolljack, the response after a Filmtone slider release. Not as VFX — as an underlayer that supports the feel of input.
